messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 61
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bus Driver
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 37

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual/Bodily Cues: Blood, Loss of Control: Lack of control, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
  Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Prevention: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
  Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Rosa's Story

Rosa was sixty-one years old and had been driving the number 7 bus route through the city for nearly thirty years. She knew every pothole on Figueroa Street, every stop where the regulars boarded, every corner where she had to brake hard. On a Tuesday afternoon in March, a sedan ran a red light at the intersection of Fifth and Main, broadsiding a minivan that had just cleared the crosswalk. Rosa was stopped at the light in her bus, three vehicles back. She watched the minivan crumple, watched a man stumble out of the sedan, watched a woman in a blue dress lying on the asphalt. There was blood—a dark spreading stain on the pavement that seemed to grow as Rosa stood frozen, unable to move, unable to call out, unable to do anything but witness.

The woman in the blue dress was Rosa's sister-in-law, Carmen. Carmen died in the hospital four hours later.

In the weeks that followed, Rosa returned to her route, but something had fractured. The sight of a red traffic light now sent a spike of dread through her chest—not fear of another accident, but a crushing certainty that she should have done something, should have warned Carmen somehow, should have been faster or braver or more present. When she saw blood on the sidewalk—a child with a scraped knee, a homeless man with a bleeding hand—the thought would crystallize: *I am a coward. I let her die.* These moments of seeing, of witnessing something that mimicked that terrible afternoon, would trigger an immediate spiral into self-recrimination so intense that Rosa would grip the steering wheel until her knuckles blanched, her mind locked on the conviction that she had failed everyone who depended on her.

The memory itself had become a kind of living thing. When it surfaced—and it surfaced without warning, at red lights, at the sound of a car horn, at the sight of anyone in a blue garment—it arrived with a violence that erased the boundary between then and now. Rosa would smell the diesel exhaust and the metallic tang of blood. She would feel the phantom pressure of her foot on the brake, hear the screech of tires. Most unsettling was that these moments came not always with clear images but sometimes as a pure, undiluted emotional avalanche: the full terror and helplessness of that afternoon pouring through her without a face or scene to anchor it, just the raw sensation of having failed, of being powerless, of being the kind of person who stands still while others die. The memory felt present, immediate, as if she were still standing at that intersection, still frozen, still complicit.

To manage the unbearable weight of these convictions—that she should have protected Carmen, that her inaction was unforgivable, that her life had become meaningless—Rosa developed rituals. Before each shift, she would count to seven while touching the steering wheel, then touch her wedding ring seven times. If she saw a car that resembled the sedan, she would mentally recite a prayer in Spanish, a bargain with God that if she performed it correctly, no one would be hurt on her route that day. She believed, with a certainty she could not quite articulate, that these rituals stood between safety and catastrophe. When she performed them, the crushing guilt would recede slightly, replaced by a fragile sense of control. When she forgot or performed them imperfectly, the guilt would surge back, more vicious than before, and the memory would flood in again—that sensory totality, that feeling of being right there on the asphalt, failing, always failing.

But the rituals demanded more. Rosa found herself unable to tolerate being touched. Her husband, Miguel, would reach for her hand and she would flinch, seized by the irrational fear that his touch would somehow break the spell, would cause the next accident. She stopped attending family dinners because she could not bear the sight of Carmen's empty chair, could not endure the reminders of her loss. The isolation deepened her conviction that she did not deserve comfort, that she should not be touched or held or forgiven. Each time she performed a ritual and still felt the weight of her guilt, each time the memory returned despite her best efforts to contain it through these private ceremonies, she would sink further into the belief that nothing could save her—not rituals, not prayer, not time. Her colleagues noticed her becoming withdrawn, saw her white-knuckling the steering wheel at intersections, heard her muttering under her breath. Two drivers had already asked if she was all right. She had no answer that made sense.

What brought Rosa to the clinic was a moment of clarity, or perhaps desperation. She had missed her granddaughter's sixth birthday party because she could not face being around children, around joy, around anything that felt like she had a right to participate in life. Sitting alone in her kitchen that evening, she realized she had become a ghost in her own home, performing rituals that no longer even convinced her, trapped in a memory that felt more real than the present, certain that she was a failure and a coward and that the world would be better off without her. She called her doctor and asked for a referral. What she wanted, more than anything, was to stop feeling like she was still standing at that intersection. What she feared most was that she would never be able to forgive herself for the person she had been on that terrible afternoon—the person who did nothing while her sister-in-law bled out on the street.
